why_use_this:
Reach for this package when you have a polynomial equation or a small system of nonlinear equations and need the actual root(s), not a symbolic simplification -- vani-algebra finds numeric real roots, it doesn't do algebra on the equations themselves (that's [vani-symbolic](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-symbolic)'s job). Quadratics are already covered by the compiler's own `f64_quadratic_root` builtin; this package's real value starts at cubic (a genuine closed-form solution via Cardano's method) and continues through arbitrary degree (via a companion-matrix eigenvalue approach) and small nonlinear systems (via Newton's method, with both an analytic-Jacobian and a finite-difference-Jacobian entry point for when you can't or don't want to hand-derive the Jacobian). If your system is *linear*, skip this package entirely and call [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix)'s `mat_solve` directly -- there's nothing here for that case. And if you need complex roots (not just real ones), this package's power-iteration eigenvalue solver won't find them -- see the README's "Scope" section for why that's a deliberate, documented limitation rather than a bug.

A couple of examples below reuse the same polynomial, \(p(x) = x^2 - 3x + 2\) (roots 1 and 2, since \(p(x)=(x-1)(x-2)\)), so you can see it move through more than one function.

algebra_poly_from_roots.intuition: If you know a polynomial's roots, you can rebuild the polynomial itself by multiplying out \((x-r_1)(x-r_2)\cdots\) -- exactly like knowing \(6 = 2\times 3\) lets you reconstruct \(6\) from its factors. This function does that multiplication one root at a time, which is convenient for building test cases: pick some roots you already know, and get the exact polynomial that has them.
algebra_poly_from_roots.example: Build the polynomial with roots \(1\) and \(2\), one factor at a time. Start with \(p_0(x) = 1\) (the empty product). Multiply in \((x-1)\): \(p_1(x) = x - 1\). Multiply in \((x-2)\): \(p_2(x) = (x-1)(x-2) = x^2 - 2x - x + 2 = x^2 - 3x + 2\). So the roots \(\{1,2\}\) rebuild to \(p(x) = x^2-3x+2\) -- check it directly: \(p(1) = 1-3+2=0\) and \(p(2)=4-6+2=0\), both roots confirmed.
algebra_poly_from_roots.why: This is the exact inverse of everything else in this package: `algebra_cubic_roots_real`/`algebra_poly_roots_real` start from coefficients and find roots; this starts from roots and finds coefficients. Composing the two (build a polynomial from chosen roots, then recover them with the root-finder) is exactly how this package's own tests validate the root-finder -- if you get your known roots back out, the round trip worked.

algebra_cubic_roots_real.intuition: A general cubic \(ax^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\) has an inconvenient \(x^2\) term getting in the way of a clean formula. Cardano's trick: shift \(x\) by a constant (\(x = t - b/3a\)) so the \(t^2\) term cancels out entirely, leaving a simpler "depressed" cubic \(t^3+pt+q=0\) with only a linear and constant term. From there, a quantity called the discriminant tells you WHICH shape of formula to use to solve for \(t\) -- one shape when there are three real roots, a different shape when there's only one.
algebra_cubic_roots_real.formula: Depress: \(t^3+pt+q=0\) via \(x=t-b/3a\). Discriminant \(\Delta = -4p^3-27q^2\). If \(\Delta\ge 0\) (three real roots), use the trigonometric formula \(t_k = 2\sqrt{-p/3}\,\cos\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\arccos\!\left(\tfrac{3q}{2p}\sqrt{-3/p}\right)-\tfrac{2\pi k}{3}\right)\); if \(\Delta<0\) (one real root), use Cardano's two-cube-root formula instead.
algebra_cubic_roots_real.example:
Solve \(x^3-7x+6=0\). Here \(a=1,b=0,c=-7,d=6\) -- since \(b=0\) already, NO shift is needed (\(x=t-0/3=t\)): this cubic is already depressed, with \(p=-7\), \(q=6\).

Compute the discriminant: \(\Delta = -4p^3-27q^2 = -4(-343) - 27(36) = 1372 - 972 = 400\). Since \(\Delta>0\), we're told to expect THREE real roots, using the trigonometric branch.

Rather than grinding through the arccos formula by hand, check the prediction directly: try \(x=1\): \(1-7+6=0\) -- a root. Try \(x=2\): \(8-14+6=0\) -- another root. Try \(x=-3\): \(-27+21+6=0\) -- a third root. Three real roots found (\(1\), \(2\), \(-3\)), exactly as the positive discriminant predicted.
algebra_cubic_roots_real.why: Knowing the discriminant's sign BEFORE solving is what lets this function pick the right formula automatically, without trial and error -- the trigonometric formula only produces real outputs when \(\Delta\ge 0\); using it on a one-real-root cubic (\(\Delta<0\)) would involve taking the arccos of a number outside \([-1,1]\), undefined for real inputs. Checking the sign first is what makes this a reliable general solver instead of a formula that only works on some inputs.

algebra_poly_companion.intuition: It's a genuinely surprising fact that you can turn "find a polynomial's roots" into "find a matrix's eigenvalues" -- two problems that look completely unrelated. The companion matrix is the bridge: a specially-shaped matrix built directly from the polynomial's coefficients, engineered so that its eigenvalues are EXACTLY the polynomial's roots. Once you have this matrix, `mat_eig_power` (built for a completely different purpose, finding a matrix's dominant eigenvalue) becomes a perfectly good root-finder for free.
algebra_poly_companion.formula: For monic \(p(x)=x^n+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0\), the \(n\times n\) companion matrix has 1s on the subdiagonal (\(C_{i,i-1}=1\)) and the negated coefficients \(-c_0,-c_1,\ldots,-c_{n-1}\) down the LAST column (row \(i\) holds \(-c_i\)).
algebra_poly_companion.example: Build the companion matrix for \(p(x)=x^2-3x+2\) (the running example above): here \(n=2\), \(c_0=2\), \(c_1=-3\). The last column (column 1) holds \(-c_0=-2\) at row 0 and \(-c_1=3\) at row 1. The subdiagonal holds a single 1 at \(C_{1,0}\). So \[ C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. \] Check its eigenvalues by hand: the characteristic equation is \(\det(C-\lambda I)=0\), i.e. \((-\lambda)(3-\lambda) - (-2)(1) = \lambda^2-3\lambda+2=0\) -- which is \(p(\lambda)=0\) itself! Factoring gives \((\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)=0\), so \(\lambda=1\) or \(\lambda=2\) -- exactly \(p(x)\)'s two roots, recovered as this small matrix's two eigenvalues.
algebra_poly_companion.why: Notice the characteristic equation you get from \(\det(C-\lambda I)\) is, by construction, identical to \(p(\lambda)\) itself -- that's not a coincidence, it's the entire design of the companion matrix. This is what lets `algebra_poly_roots_real` handle ANY degree by reusing `mat_eig_power`'s eigenvalue-finding machinery instead of needing a separate hand-derived formula for degree 4, 5, 6, and beyond (which, past degree 4, provably can't even exist in closed form -- the Abel-Ruffini theorem).

algebra_newton_system.intuition: Newton's method for a single equation walks downhill using the slope at your current guess; for a SYSTEM of equations, "slope" becomes the Jacobian matrix (every equation's sensitivity to every variable at once), and "walk downhill" becomes "solve a small linear system to find which direction simultaneously reduces every equation's error."
algebra_newton_system.formula: \[ x_{k+1} = x_k - J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k) \] computed by solving \(J(x_k)\,\delta = -F(x_k)\) for \(\delta\) (via `mat_solve`, never by explicitly inverting \(J\)), then setting \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\delta\).
algebra_newton_system.example:
Find where the unit circle \(F_1(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1=0\) meets the line \(F_2(x,y)=x-y=0\), starting from the guess \((1,1)\).

The Jacobian is \(J = \begin{pmatrix}2x & 2y\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\); at \((1,1)\): \(J=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). And \(F(1,1) = (1^2+1^2-1,\ 1-1) = (1,\,0)\).

Solve \(J\delta=-F\), i.e. \(\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta_x\\\delta_y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\). The second row gives \(\delta_x-\delta_y=0\), so \(\delta_x=\delta_y\). Substituting into the first row: \(2\delta_x+2\delta_x=-1\), so \(\delta_x=\delta_y=-0.25\).

New point: \((1-0.25,\ 1-0.25) = (0.75,\ 0.75)\). The true intersection is \((1/\sqrt2, 1/\sqrt2)\approx(0.7071,\,0.7071)\) -- one Newton step already moved from \((1,1)\) (distance \(\approx0.41\) from the true answer) to \((0.75,0.75)\) (distance \(\approx0.06\)), a big jump toward the answer from a single linear solve.
algebra_newton_system.why: Each Newton step here costs one Jacobian evaluation plus one linear solve (`mat_solve`, \(O(n^3)\)) -- expensive per step compared to a gradient-only method, but the quadratic convergence rate near the answer (the error roughly SQUARES each step once you're close) usually more than makes up for it in the total number of steps needed.

algebra_newton_system_damped.intuition: Plain Newton's method always takes the FULL step the linear solve suggests, which can badly overshoot if the current guess is far from the answer (the Jacobian's straight-line prediction stops being a good approximation of the actual curved function once you've moved too far). Damping adds a safety check: before committing to the full step, see if it actually helps; if not, try half the step, then a quarter, and so on, until one actually reduces the error.
algebra_newton_system_damped.formula: \[ x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha\,\delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = -J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k) \] where \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) is found by backtracking (halving from \(\alpha=1\)) until \(\lVert F(x_k+\alpha\delta_k)\rVert < \lVert F(x_k)\rVert\) or the iteration cap is hit.
algebra_newton_system_damped.example: Reusing `algebra_newton_system`'s step, \(\delta=(-0.25,-0.25)\) from \((1,1)\): try the full step first, \(\alpha=1\), landing at \((0.75,0.75)\). Check whether \(\lVert F(0.75,0.75)\rVert\) is smaller than \(\lVert F(1,1)\rVert = \lVert(1,0)\rVert = 1\): \(F(0.75,0.75) = (0.75^2+0.75^2-1,\ 0) = (0.125,\ 0)\), so \(\lVert F(0.75,0.75)\rVert=0.125\), much smaller than 1 -- the full step is accepted immediately, no halving needed this time.
algebra_newton_system_damped.why: In this particular example the full Newton step already happened to help, so damping made no visible difference -- but for a worse-conditioned system or a guess far from any root, a full Newton step can genuinely increase the error (even flip to a wildly different, wrong region), and that's exactly the case backtracking exists to catch: reject the overshooting step and retry smaller before accepting anything.

algebra_newton_system_fd.intuition: `algebra_newton_system` needs the caller to hand it an exact Jacobian function -- fine when you can differentiate \(F\) by hand, but sometimes \(F\) is complicated enough that deriving its Jacobian is tedious or error-prone. The finite-difference variant sidesteps that entirely: it estimates each Jacobian entry by nudging one variable slightly and seeing how much each equation's output changes, the same idea `vani-calculus`'s `diff_central`/`diff_forward` use for a single-variable derivative, just applied one column at a time.
algebra_newton_system_fd.formula: \[ J_{ij} \approx \dfrac{F_i(x+he_j) - F_i(x)}{h} \] for a small step \(h\) and the \(j\)-th standard basis vector \(e_j\) (i.e. nudge only variable \(j\)).
algebra_newton_system_fd.example: Estimate \(J_{11}=\partial F_1/\partial x\) at \((1,1)\) for \(F_1(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1\), using \(h=0.01\): \(F_1(1,1) = 1\) (computed earlier). Nudge \(x\) by \(h\): \(F_1(1.01,\,1) = 1.01^2+1^2-1 = 1.0201+1-1=1.0201\). So \(J_{11}\approx\dfrac{1.0201-1}{0.01} = 2.01\) -- very close to the true analytic value \(\partial F_1/\partial x = 2x = 2\) at \(x=1\), off by only 0.01 because \(h\) isn't infinitesimally small.
algebra_newton_system_fd.why: Building the full Jacobian this way costs \(n\) extra evaluations of \(F\) per Newton step (one nudge per variable) on top of evaluating \(F\) itself -- more expensive per step than `algebra_newton_system`'s analytic path, and slightly less accurate (that small \(0.01\) error above compounds over iterations), but it's the only option when you don't have or don't want to hand-derive an exact Jacobian.
